stances.claim: Lawyer Theodore O. Te's 52-page petition seeks the cancellation of Bongbong's COC (under Sections 74 and 78 OEC) on two grounds of false material representation: (a) paragraph 11 declaring eligibility despite the CA's October 31, 1997 conviction making him ineligible to hold public office; (b) Item 22 denying past liability for an offense carrying the accessory penalty of perpetual disqualification under PD 1994 / NIRC Section 253.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-ground petition restatement (faithful summary as analytical baseline)

stances.claim: The CA decision merely affirmed the RTC judgments of July 27, 1995, and the CA's 'inexplicable' omission of the RTC-imposed imprisonment penalty (retaining only fines) does not eliminate the accessory penalty of disqualification because that accessory attaches to a conviction regardless of the main penalty imposed.
stances.rhetorical_move: accessory-penalty-survives-main-penalty-modification doctrine (preserving the disqualification through the CA's penalty reduction)

stances.claim: Mendoza's 7-page Answer simply asserts that the Petition is 'bereft of any specific allegation of a material representation,' that the Comelec should take judicial notice of BB's prior elective positions, that he 'has all the qualifications of a President,' and that the CA did not convict him of moral turpitude -- and prays for face-to-face argument and dismissal.
stances.rhetorical_move: petition-vs-Answer face-off framing (presenting each pleading's core posture neutrally before later analytical pivot)

stances.claim: If Bongbong's COC is cancelled or denied due course, HE CANNOT BE SUBSTITUTED because such cancellation legally means that the COC never existed; therefore Bongbong's votes will not be counted, and the candidate getting the highest number of votes excluding his would be declared winner.
stances.rhetorical_move: consequence-mapping with emphatic ALL-CAPS prohibition ('HE CANNOT BE SUBSTITUTED' as the column's central operative claim)

stances.claim: Contrary to media reports and 'analysts,' Te's petition seeks cancellation, NOT disqualification -- and the difference matters: disqualification under Section 68 OEC is available only for election offenses defined by the OEC, not by other penal laws, and disqualification permits substitution by another candidate from the same party bearing the same surname; cancellation does not.
stances.rhetorical_move: media-correction with doctrinal-precision insistence (rebuking imprecise 'analysts' as analytically central)

stances.claim: Two important future-column questions are flagged: (i) elaboration on the parties' positions on the merits, and (ii) what happens if Bongbong's COC is cancelled AFTER Congress declares him president-elect, or AFTER he takes his oath as President.
stances.rhetorical_move: future-column teaser (deferring resolution while signaling analytical agenda)

notable_anecdotes: The 52-page-vs-7-page page-count contrast between Te's petition and Mendoza's Answer -- a quietly diagnostic detail about the parties' relative procedural posture and burden of argument.

CJ's correction of media outlets and 'analysts' (with the scare quotes) for conflating cancellation with disqualification -- making this column the analytical reference point for a doctrinal distinction routinely muddled in 2022-election coverage.

The ALL-CAPS 'HE CANNOT BE SUBSTITUTED' as the column's central operative claim -- one of CJ's most emphatic typographic interventions in his COC-series columns, demarcating the cancellation route's substitution-blocking consequence.

The 'inexplicably omitted the penalty of imprisonment' phrasing characterizing the 1997 CA's penalty reduction -- a quietly loaded adverb capturing CJ's puzzlement at the CA's penalty modification without overt accusation.

Two future-column teasers in one column ('I will expound in a future column'; 'Ah, the answer also merits a future column') -- establishing the COC analysis as a multi-installment arc that the subsequent A165 / A164 / A163 columns would complete.

The note that BB's CA conviction affirmed RTC judgments rendered on July 27, 1995 -- a date that anchors the entire eligibility analysis in the trial court's original judgment day, twenty-six years before the 2022 COC.

one_paragraph_summary: Following up on his November 14 column 'The Bongbong-Sara juggernaut,' Panganiban opens his Bongbong Marcos COC analytical series with a doctrinal map. He summarizes lawyer Theodore O. Te's 52-page petition before the Comelec, which seeks to cancel Bongbong's October 6, 2021 COC on two grounds of false material representation: paragraph 11 declared 'eligible for the office I seek to be elected to' despite the Court of Appeals' final judgment of October 31, 1997 (affirming the RTC judgments of July 27, 1995) convicting BB for failure to file ITRs for 1982-1985, and Item 22 denied past liability for an offense carrying the accessory penalty of perpetual disqualification. The petition argues that PD 1994 (effective January 1, 1986; now Section 253 of the 1997 NIRC) attaches the accessory penalty regardless of the CA's 'inexplicable' omission of the RTC-imposed imprisonment penalty. Bongbong's counter-pleading -- Estelito P. Mendoza's seven-page Answer -- simply posits that the Petition is 'bereft of any specific allegation of a material representation,' asks the Comelec to take judicial notice of BB's prior elective positions and presidential qualifications, denies any CA finding of moral turpitude, and prays for face-to-face argument. Panganiban defers the merits analysis but makes one crucial doctrinal point: if Bongbong's COC is cancelled, 'HE CANNOT BE SUBSTITUTED' because cancellation legally means that the COC never existed -- his votes will not be counted, and the next highest vote-getter would be declared winner. Contrary to media reports and 'analysts,' the petition seeks cancellation under Section 78 (false material representation), NOT disqualification under Section 68 (which is available only for election offenses defined by the OEC and DOES allow substitution by another candidate from the same party bearing the same surname). He closes with two teaser questions for future columns: what would happen if Bongbong's COC were cancelled AFTER Congress declares him president-elect, or AFTER he takes his oath as President?
